notes.meaning: Moses tells the Israelites not to panic when they face enemies with horses, chariots, and larger armies. Israel fought on foot, but their true strength was the Lord. God had already delivered them from the mighty power of Egypt, proving He could protect them anywhere.

When the army prepares to march into battle, a priest steps forward to address the troops. In Israel's covenant community, the priest represented God and spoke His blessing over the soldiers. This reminded the people that they could only fight in wars that honored the Lord.

The priest calls the men to listen and commands them not to lose heart, tremble, or panic before the enemy. Hostile armies used shouting, clashing weapons, and thundering chariots to terrify their opponents. God told His people to stand firm against fear because their confidence rested in Him.

The priest explains that the Lord Himself marches with Israel to fight against their enemies and give them the victory. The ark of the covenant, the symbol of God's presence, often traveled with the army as a reminder that He was near. Real safety came from God, not from weapons or military power.

The officers announce an exemption for any man who has built a new house but has not yet dedicated it. Dedicating a home meant moving in and holding a joyful gathering to thank God for His blessing. The Lord showed kindness by sending such a man home, so he would not die in battle before enjoying the fruit of his labor.

The officers also excuse any soldier who planted a vineyard but has not yet eaten its fruit. Under the law, fruit trees could not be harvested for common use until their fifth year. God cared about ordinary family life and did not want a person to lose what he had worked hard to plant.

A man who was engaged to be married was also permitted to go home from the army. Betrothal was a binding promise of marriage, and dying in battle would mean losing his bride and leaving no children behind. This law protected new families and showed great care for human relationships.

The officers make one more announcement, sending away anyone who feels terrified or faint of heart. Fear spreads fast, and a panicking soldier could easily destroy the courage of the entire company. God wanted a willing army of confident fighters rather than a large crowd of frightened men.

After all the excused men depart, the officers place commanders in charge of the remaining soldiers. Even though God gave the victory, the army still needed good order and trusted human leaders. Faith in God's power works together with wise preparation and teamwork.

Before attacking a city, the Israelites were required to make a formal offer of peace. This rule applied to distant foreign cities outside the Promised Land, showing that God wanted to avoid bloodshed whenever possible. Israel was commanded to seek peace first before taking up arms.

If the city accepted the terms of peace and opened its gates, the inhabitants were spared from death. The people became tribute-paying laborers who served Israel instead of being destroyed. This permitted both sides to live in peace without violence.

If the enemy rejected the offer of peace and chose war, Israel was to surround the city and place it under siege. A siege cut off food and water until the walled town could be captured. The city brought this hardship upon itself by refusing the path of peace.

differ.view: Reformed teaching often sees the command to kill all the men as a temporary concession to human hardness of heart, falling short of God's perfect law of love while still restraining greater cruelty.

notes.meaning: When the Lord delivered the resisting city into Israel's hands, the soldiers put all the adult men to death. These men were the fighters who had refused peace and chosen to battle against God's people. Slaying the male soldiers protected Israel from future rebellions and attacks.

notes.meaning: The women, children, livestock, and goods of the captured city were spared and taken as plunder. The Israelites were allowed to use these provisions to support their families and cover the costs of war. Spared lives and captured goods showed that not everyone in the city was treated as a combatant.

Moses emphasizes that these rules of offering peace and taking plunder applied only to distant cities. They governed ordinary wars fought beyond the borders of the Promised Land. Different instructions applied to the corrupt nations living inside Canaan itself.

Inside the land God gave Israel as an inheritance, the soldiers were not to leave any person alive. The cities of the Canaanite nations were placed under complete judgment. God gave this strict order to clear out severe corruption and make the land a holy home for His people.

Moses lists six Canaanite nations that were to be completely destroyed as the Lord commanded. This destruction was a unique divine judgment against societies that had practiced extreme cruelty and wicked rituals for generations. Israel carried out this judgment as God's appointed instrument, not out of personal greed or malice.

The main purpose of destroying these nations was to protect Israel from their spiritual wickedness. If the Canaanites remained, they would teach Israel to worship idols through evil practices like child sacrifice. Removing these corrupt influences protected the covenant people from falling into ruin.

During a long siege, the Israelites were forbidden to cut down fruit trees to build military barriers. Fruit trees provided food to sustain human life, and chopping them down would harm the land for years to come. Trees were not enemy soldiers, so they were not to be treated as enemies.

The soldiers were allowed to cut down only non-fruit trees to build siege works against the defending city until it fell. This gave Israel the wood they needed for military engines and ramps without destroying their future food supply. God taught His people to conduct warfare with discipline and care for the land.
